'''''Alluaudia procera''''', or '''Madagascar ocotillo''', is a [[deciduous]] [[succulent plant]] [[species]] of the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Didiereaceae]]. It is [[endemic]] to south [[Madagascar]].<ref name=q>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=6237 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref>

==Description==
This plant is a spiny succulent shrub, with thick water-storing stems and leaves that are deciduous in the long dry season.  Although strikingly similar in appearance, it is not closely related to the [[ocotillo]], ''[[Fouquieria splendens]]'' of the [[Sonoran Desert]]s in North America.
[[File:Alluaudia procera kz02.jpg|thumb]]

Young alluaudias form a tangle of stems that last for several years, after which a strong central stem develops. The basal stems then die out, leaving a tree-like stem that branches higher up on the main trunk. This main stem can grow up to 15m tall. The stems are covered in green oval leaves, measuring an average of 2.5cm long. The small green-yellow flowers grow in clusters on the tops of stems.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.kew.org/plants/madagascar-ocotillo | title= Madagascar ocotillo | website=kew.org |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=21 November 2025}}</ref>

Like other members of family Didiereaceae, the leaves of ''Alluaudia'', produced from brachyblasts similar to the areoles found in cacti, are small, appear single and are accompanied with conical spines. Its flowers are unisexual and radially symmetric. 
[[File:Alluaudia procera leaves.jpg|thumb|''Alluaudia procera'' closeup of stem and leaves.]]

==Taxonomy==
The Didiereaceae comprise 11 species divided into 4 genera, of which the largest is ''[[Alluaudia]]'' (six species). Alluaudia has been subdivided into the 2 sections ''Alluaudia'' and ''Androyella''.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rabesa|first1=Zafera Antoine|title=Definition de deux sections du genre Alluaudia (Didiereaceae)|journal=Taxon|date=1982|volume=31|issue=4|pages=339–358|doi=10.2307/1219699|jstor=1219699}}</ref> In this way, ''Alluaudia procera'' has two sisters, ''[[Alluaudia ascendens]]'' and ''[[Alluaudia montagnacii]]''.

Based on molecular phylogeny conducted<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Applequist|first1=W. L.|title=Phylogeny of the Madagascan endemic family Didiereaceae|journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution|date=2000|volume=221|issue=3–4|pages=157–166|doi=10.1007/bf01089291|s2cid=33830803}}</ref> ''[[Alluaudia]]'', ''Alluaudiopsis'', and ''Didierea'' from the family are all supported as monophyletic. Relationships within the genus ''Alluaudia'' are relevant to the evolution of polyploidy within the family.

Researchers haven't figured out where the family Didiereaceae originates. However, the nearest relative of the Didiereaceae, ''Calyptrotheca somalensis'', is endemic to East Africa,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Nyananyo|first1=B. L.|title=The systematic position of the genus Calyptrotheca Gilg (Portulacaceae)|journal=Feddes Repertorium |date=1986|volume=97|issue=11–12|pages=767–769|doi=10.1002/fedr.4910971109|doi-access=free}}</ref> from which the island of Madagascar separated 100 million years ago.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Raven|first1=Peter H.|last2=Axelrod|first2=Daniel I.|title=Angiosperm biogeography and past continental movements|journal=Ann. Missouri Bot. Gard.|date=1974|volume=61|issue=3|pages=539–673|doi=10.2307/2395021|jstor=2395021}}</ref> Thus, the Didiereaceae may have originated from the dispersal to Madagascar of a ''Calyptrotheca''-like East African ancestor.
